content: The importance of outcomes for individuals or populations affected by soil-transmitted helminth infections was assessed by reviewing qualitative data on how end-users, including children, adolescent girls, women of reproductive age, and pregnant women, perceive these infections, deworming interventions, and their effects. This information was presented during the guideline development group meeting. In cases where there was uncertainty or variability in the values and preferences of the target beneficiaries, a conditional recommendation was considered appropriate. The acceptability of interventions was evaluated by reviewing qualitative data on how healthcare workers and service providers perceive soil-transmitted helminths, preventive chemotherapy, and their effects on at-risk groups. This information was also presented during the guideline development meeting. Higher acceptability among stakeholders increased the likelihood of a clear recommendation. For interventions with low acceptability, strategies to address concerns during implementation were discussed. Resource use was analyzed to determine how resource-intensive and costly the intervention would be for service users and health systems in various settings. Recommendations were more likely to be made when resource implications were clearly advantageous or disadvantageous. Conditional recommendations were considered when resource implications were uncertain. Interventions were more likely to be recommended if they were expected to reduce health inequities among different groups of women and their families. Feasibility was assessed by presenting examples of deworming implementation in at-risk groups across different settings, highlighting potential barriers. Greater feasibility increased the likelihood of a recommendation. Each recommendation was supported by a rationale, implementation considerations, and research priorities based on discussions during the guideline development meeting. Decision-making procedures were established at the start of the meeting, with Dr. Biggs and Professor Nesheim nominated and approved as chairpersons. At least two-thirds of the group participated in initial discussions of evidence and proposed recommendations. Voting was conducted via a secret ballot using an online form, and abstentions were not allowed. If unanimous consensus was not reached, further deliberations and a second round of voting were conducted. A two-thirds majority was required for approval if consensus was still not achieved. Voting results will be retained by WHO for up to five years. The guideline's first draft was prepared by the responsible technical officer with input from the steering group. Technical editing and proofreading were performed by a contracted party. Peer reviewers were selected after assessing declarations of interest, and five out of eight approached reviewers agreed to participate. The guideline will be disseminated through the WHO website, including the WHO Nutrition and Neglected Tropical Diseases websites, and the e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA). It will also be shared with international partners, WHO country and regional offices, ministries of health, collaborating centers, universities, other UN agencies, and NGOs. The WHO steering group will monitor research developments in preventive chemotherapy for at-risk groups, particularly in areas where evidence quality was low or very low. If the guideline requires updating or its validity is questioned, the Department of Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases will coordinate the update following WHO's formal guideline development procedures. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, WHO departments and internal partners will conduct a search for new evidence.
